title: Demonstrate an understanding of how scientific skills and knowledge could contribute to sustainable use of resources

lessons.title: Resources and what sustainable means
lessons.html:
Our natural resources

A resource is something from nature that people use. On a farm the most important resources are soil, water, plants, animals, air and energy. Some resources can grow back or be replaced. These are called renewable, for example grass, trees, and water from rain. Others cannot be replaced once they are used up. These are non-renewable, for example diesel, petrol and coal.

What is sustainable use?

Sustainable use means using resources in a way that leaves enough for the future. Our children and grandchildren must also be able to farm the same land. If we overgraze the veld, plough steep slopes or waste water, the land becomes poor and future farmers will suffer.

Signs that resources are being misused

  • Dongas (deep gullies) where soil has washed away.
  • Bare veld with few good grasses and many weeds or bush.
  • Rivers and dams full of mud after rain.
  • Boreholes that dry up because too much water was pumped.
  • Rubbish and chemical containers left in the veld.

The law helps protect resources

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 is about protecting soil, water and vegetation on farmland. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 controls how water is used. Farmers must follow these laws.

Example

A farmer in the Eastern Cape kept too many sheep in one camp for years. The grass disappeared and the soil washed away in the summer storms. Now the camp can carry far fewer animals. If he had moved the sheep between camps and rested the veld, the grass would have recovered.

lessons.title: Using science to look after resources
lessons.html:
Science skills on the farm

Science is a way of finding out how things work by observing, measuring, testing and recording. You do not need a laboratory. Farmers use science skills every day.

Scientific skills

  1. Observe: look carefully. Which plants are yellow? Where does water collect after rain?
  2. Measure: use a rain gauge, a thermometer, a measuring jug or a scale. Write down the numbers.
  3. Ask a question: for example, will this field give more maize if we add compost?
  4. Test: try compost on one part of the field and not on the other part. Keep everything else the same.
  5. Record and compare: weigh the harvest from both parts and compare.
  6. Conclude and share: decide what worked and tell others.

How science helps use resources wisely

ResourceScience-based practice
SoilSoil tests show which nutrients are missing, so you only add the fertiliser that is needed. Contour ploughing and cover crops reduce erosion.
WaterDrip irrigation and soil moisture checks give plants only the water they need.
VeldMeasuring grass cover helps decide how many animals a camp can carry, and when to rest it.
PestsScouting and counting pests shows when spraying is really needed, so less chemical is used.
EnergySolar pumps and panels use the sun instead of diesel.

Reduce, reuse, recycle

Make compost from crop leftovers and manure instead of burning them. Reuse clean containers for safe purposes only. Never reuse empty chemical containers for food or water; return them as the label or supplier says.

Key points

  • Resources are renewable (grass, water) or non-renewable (diesel, coal).
  • Sustainable use leaves enough resources for the future.
  • Science skills are observe, measure, test, record and conclude.
  • Soil tests, drip irrigation and veld measurements help use resources wisely.
  • Laws such as Act 43 of 1983 and the National Water Act protect resources.
